'''Mordehai Heiblum''' ({{Langx|he|מוטי הייבלום}} – sometimes called '''Moty Heiblum''', born May 25, 1947, in [[Holon]]) is an Israeli electrical engineer and condensed matter physicist, known for his research in [[mesoscopic physics]]. His experimental techniques allowed to demonstrate the fractional charge of the [[fractional quantum Hall effect]] and measuring the of half-integer [[thermal conductance quantum]] at filling fraction 5/2. For these discoveries he earned several prizes, including the 2025 [[Wolf Prize in Physics]].<ref name=":0" />

He was elected a Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2025.<ref>https://www.nasonline.org/news/2025-nas-election/</ref>
==Biography==
Moty Heiblum was born and raised in Holon. His mother was the only Holocaust survivor in her immediate family, and most of his father's family perished in the Holocaust. From 1967 to 1971 Moty Heiblum served in the [[Israeli Defense Force]] (IDF) in the IDF Communications Corps and was an instructor at the IDF Air Force Technical School. Heiblum graduated in electrical engineering from the [[Technion]] with a bachelor's degree in 1973 and from [[Carnegie-Mellon University]] with a master's degree in 1974.<ref name=briefbio1987>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QdhFAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA2-PA680| title=Review of budget proposals for fiscal year 1988: Hearings before the Committee on the Budget, House of Representatives, One hundredth Congress, first session | page=680 | year=1987 }}</ref> He received in 1978 his Ph.D. with thesis ''Characteristics of metal-oxide-metal devices''<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3H-Dw7hhgIgC&pg=PA2519| page=2519 | title=Scientific and Technical Aerospace Reports | volume=17, Issues 17-20 | year=1979 }}</ref> supervised by [[John Roy Whinnery]].<ref name=academictree>{{cite web|title=Moty Heiblum|website=academictree.org|url=https://academictree.org/math/peopleinfo.php?pid=431295}}</ref> After completing his Ph.D., Heiblum joined the IBM [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]].<ref name=briefbio1987/>

After working at the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center for 12 years, Heiblum returned in 1990 to Israel and established at the Weizmann Institute, with the support of Professor [[Yoseph Imry]], the Joseph H. and Belle R. Braun Center for Submicron Research with the mission to "study and develop submicron semiconductor structures working in the mesoscopic regime."<ref>{{cite web|title=Submicron Center|website=Weizmann Institute|url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/condmat/submicron/}}</ref> The initial investment for the Submicron Center was approximately $16 million. Heiblum has headed the Submicron Center since its founding in 1990. That same year he was appointed a full professor at the Weizmann Institute. He established the Department of Condensed Matter Physics at the Weizmann Institute and was its first director from 1993 to 1996 and from 2007 to 2012 he was again its director. In 2000 he was appointed to the Alex and Ida Susan Professorial Chair of Submicron Studies.

From 1991 to 1992, Heiblum headed a government committee that advised the Minister of Science on how to encourage the microelectronics industry in the State of Israel. Since 2001, he has chaired the board of directors of [[Braude College of Engineering]]. From 1993 to 1996, he was a visiting professor for several weeks each summer at the [[TU Wien|Vienna University of Technology]]. From 1996 to 1997 he was on sabbatical as a visiting professor at Stanford University in combination with [[Hewlett Packard Labs]] in [[Palo Alto, California]]. He was an editor for the journal ''[[Semiconductor Science and Technology]]'' and is now an editor for the journal ''[[Solid State Communications]]''. He organized and conducted, in collaboration with Professor Elisha Cohen of the Technion, the 1998 International Conference of Semiconductors, which was attended by about 1,100 people and held in Jerusalem.

His doctoral students include [[Amir Yacoby]], graduated in 1994.<ref name="academictree" />

== Research ==
The main focus of Heiblum's research is the quantum behavior of electrons in high-purity mesoscopic materials, and especially the [[quantum Hall effect]] (QHE) regime. Noteworthy highlights of the research done by him and his group are "novel electronic interferometers – demonstrating [[Wave interference#Quantum interference|one-electron and two-electron interference]]; which-path detectors – allowing to turn 'on and off' electrons' coherence; detection of [[Fractional quantum Hall effect|fractional charge]]s via sensitive [[shot noise]] measurements; and observation of quantized heat flow in the fractional abelian and non-abelian states in the QHE regime."<ref name=BuckleyPrize>{{cite web|title=2021 Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Physics Prize Recipient, Moty Heiblum|website=American Physical Society|url=https://aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Heiblum&first_nm=Mordehai%20(Moty)&year=2021}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

== Awards ==
He received in 1986 the IBM Outstanding Innovation Award and in 2013 the [[EMET Prize]].<ref name=BuckleyPrize/> He was elected a life fellow of the [[IEEE]], a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (1990),<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1990&unit_id=&institution=Weizmann+Institute+of+Science}} (search on year=1990 and institution=Weizmann Institute of Science)</ref> and a member of [[Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities]] (2008). In 2008, he received the [[Rothschild Prize]] in physics.<ref name=BuckleyPrize/>

In 2021, he was the single recipient of the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] with citation:
{{blockquote|For discoveries, enabled by ingenious experimental methods, of novel quantum electronic phenomena in mesoscopic and quantum Hall systems, including observation and interpretation of one-electron and two-electron interference, charge fractionalization, and quantized heat conductance in fractional Hall states.<ref name=BuckleyPrize/>}}

In 2025, he was announced as the co-recipient of the [[Wolf Prize in Physics]] together with [[Jainendra K. Jain]] (Penn State) and [[James P. Eisenstein]] (CalTech) for laying the foundation to the understanding of the [[fractional quantum Hall effect]].<ref name=":0">[https://wolffund.org.il/mordehai-moty-heiblum/ Wolf Prize in Physics 2025]</ref>

== Family ==
Moty Heiblum's wife Rachel has a PhD in biology from the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Heiblum, Rachel|website=isni.oclc.org|url=https://isni.oclc.org/xslt/DB=1.2/SET=4/TTL=1/CMD?ACT=SRCH&IKT=8006&SRT=LST_nd&TRM=heiblum%2C+rachel}}</ref> She worked in the Faculty of Agriculture of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem's [[Rehovot]] campus. They have four children. He has a younger brother, Zohar Heiblum, who is a director, manager, turn-around specialist, and investor in the high-tech industry.<ref>{{cite web|title=Zohar Heiblum biography|website=wallmine.com|url=https://wallmine.com/nasdaq/trpx/officer/1951031/zohar-heiblum}}</ref>
